newsitem.title: JAPAN: Exports boost Japan car output in first half 1997.
newsitem.headline: Exports boost Japan car output in first half 1997.

text.p: Japan's vehicle production in the first half of 1997 rose from the year-ago period, as a weak yen boosted exports, an industry group said Thursday, but analysts expect output to grow slower in the second half of the year.
The Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA) said vehicle production climbed 12.1 percent to 5.70 million units in the first half of 1997.
Output in June, at 977,625 vehicles, was up a brisk 16.1 percent from the same month last year, its biggest monthly gain since a sales tax increase on April 1.
"Production increased because the weak yen helped boost Japan's vehicle exports and because production last year was relatively low due to the strong yen," a JAMA official said.

He added that, if the first half's high growth rate in exports continues, Japan's 1997 output will reach 11 million units. Production in 1996 totalled 10.35 million vehicles units, rising for the first time in six years.
Analysts expected growth to slow in the second half of the year, however, although the total for 1997 is likely to surpass last year's figure.

They said Japan cannot continue its fast pace of export growth, citing weakening demand in Thailand and other Asian countries, a rise in Japanese carmakers' inventories abroad and concerns about trade friction with the United States.
Nobuaki Yanachi, a senior analyst for Kankaku Research, estimated Japan's domestic vehicle production at 10.90 million units in 1997.
Seiji Sugiura, a car industry analyst at Nomura Securities Co Ltd's research unit, estimated vehicle output at 10.80 million units.
The analysts also said the recovery in domestic vehicle demand is likely to be slower than they had previously expected, a view that was echoed by industry officials.

"Japan's vehicle demand is still weak. The number of visitors to showrooms has increased (in recent months), but that has not resulted in an increase in actual sales, mainly because of the impact of the sales tax increase," Toyota Executive Vice President Kanji Kurioka said in a recent interview.

Industry sources said Japan's domestic vehicle sales in the first 23 days of July fell 13.3 percent from the year-ago period. Japanese domestic vehicle sales have been posting monthly declines since April, when Japan raised its national sales tax to 5 percent from 3 percent.

The JAMA official said, however, that Japanese carmakers' plans to introduce several new models in and after August of this year, ahead of Tokyo motor show in late October and early November, would help buoy domestic demand.

In the first half of 1997, domestic production by Toyota Motor Corp., Japan's top carmaker, rose 9.7 percent from a year earlier to 1.83 million units, followed by Nissan Motor Co. Ltd. at 906,851, up 14.1 percent, Mitsubishi Motors Corp. at 656,349, up 10.5 percent, Honda Motor Co. Ltd. at 648,814, up 26.6 percent, and Mazda Motor Corp. at 445,501, up 14.8 percent.
